summary: The note is a Wikipedia article describing the flail mower, a powered vegetation cutter for heavier grass and scrub than a normal lawn mower can handle. It explains that most flail mowers are PTO-driven implements attached to tractor three-point hitches, how the rotating horizontal drum and flails work, and how flail mowers differ from toppers. It also covers hedge-cutting and robust forestry variants called flail mulchers, shredders or choppers.
one_line: Overview of the flail mower, a PTO-driven or self-powered vegetation cutter for rough grass and brambles, and how it differs from a topper.
key_facts: A flail mower is a type of powered garden/agricultural equipment used to deal with heavier grass/scrub which a normal lawn mower could not cope with.
Many flail mowers are PTO driven implements that can attach to the three-point hitches found on the rear of most tractors.
Flail mowers are best used to provide a rough cut to long grass and even brambles in locations such as roadsides, where contact with loose debris may be possible.
The flail mower gets its name from flails attached to its rotating horizontal drum, also called tube, rotor, or axle.
Many implement companies also refer to the flails as knives, blades or hammers.
The rows of flails are usually staggered to give a continuous cut for reduced wear on the machine.
The rotating drum is parallel to the axle of the tractor, so the PTO driveshaft must make a right angle through a gearbox to transfer rotational energy to the drum.
As the drum rotates, centrifugal force pushes the flails outward.
Standard flails are shaped like an extruded "T" or "Y" and a chain attaches to the bottom.
If a flail strikes an immovable object, it simply bounces off, whereas other rotary mowers may grab and throw small objects out of the mower deck.
Flail mowers may be used in a more or less upright position for trimming the sides of hedges, and are then often called hedge cutters or hedge trimmers.
Robust flail mower variants used in forestry and agroforestry are called flail mulchers, flail shredders, or flail choppers.
Flail mowers cut grass very short and fine and can handle rough uneven surfaces, whereas a topper is mostly used to top off growth such as weeds and long grass.
The topper uses swinging blades instead of rotating blades, and its mulch is finer than the larger mulch a flail mower produces.
Flail mowers are much more versatile in use but do cost more than toppers.
